sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Belt Squat is a lower-body exercise performed on a specialized machine where resistance is loaded through a belt attached around the waist rather than across the shoulders or back.

This setup allows the lifter to train the legs heavily while removing compressive load from the spine.

Belt squats are popular for building leg strength and hypertrophy, especially for lifters with back issues or those wanting to add volume without additional axial loading.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Loads the legs without compressing the spine
- Ideal for lifters with lower back issues or fatigue
- Allows heavy leg training on recovery days
- Strong emphasis on quads, glutes, and hamstrings
- Easier to maintain an upright torso than a barbell squat
- Great accessory movement for powerlifters and athletes
- Can be used for high-volume hypertrophy work

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Quadriceps, Glutes, Hamstrings

Secondary: Adductors, Calves, Core

sections.heading: Set Up
sections.content:
1. Adjust the height of the machine's platform to match your body height.
2. Ensure that the weight stack or loading mechanism is set to the desired resistance level.
3. Check that safety pins and lever arms are properly positioned.

sections.heading: Attach the Belt
sections.content:
1. Put on the provided belt or harness and secure it around your waist.
2. Make sure it is snug but not uncomfortably tight.
3. Confirm the attachment point is centered on the front of the belt.

sections.heading: Stand on the Platform
sections.content:
1. Step onto the machine's platform with your feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Position yourself so the weight stack is between your legs and the belt is securely attached to your waist.
3. Stand tall with chest up and core braced before unracking the load.

sections.heading: Squat
sections.content:
1. Initiate the squat by bending at your hips and knees.
2. Keep your back straight, chest up, and core engaged as you lower your body down.
3. Lower yourself until your thighs are parallel to the ground or as far as your mobility allows.

sections.heading: Return to Standing
sections.content:
1. Exhale as you push through your heels and extend your hips and knees, lifting the weight stack or resistance.
2. Stand back up to the starting position.
3. Keep your movements controlled and maintain good form throughout the exercise.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Belt positioned too high or too low on the hips
- Rounding the lower back at the bottom of the rep
- Knees caving inward during the descent or ascent
- Not reaching adequate depth
- Using too much weight and cutting range of motion
- Leaning excessively forward instead of staying upright
- Bouncing out of the bottom position

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Belt Squat Machine (plate-loaded or selectorized)
- Weight Plates (if plate-loaded)
- Belt or Harness (usually provided with the machine)
- Flat-soled or weightlifting shoes
- Optional: Lifting Belt for core support

sections.heading: Machine Adjustments
sections.content:
1. Adjust platform height so the belt attachment aligns with your hips when standing tall.
2. Set safety stops or end ranges if the machine allows.
3. Load the desired resistance onto the weight stack or loading pin.
4. Check that the lever arm or cable path moves smoothly before beginning.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out.
2. Belt: Snug around the waist/hips, centered over the loading point.
3. Torso: Upright, chest tall, core braced.
4. Head: Neutral, eyes forward.
5. Grip: Hold the handles lightly for balance, not to pull yourself up.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Barbell Back Squat: Traditional loaded squat with bar on the back
- Hack Squat Machine: Machine-based squat with fixed path
- Leg Press: Seated press variation for quad and glute work
- Goblet Squat: Front-loaded squat with dumbbell or kettlebell
- Bulgarian Split Squat: Unilateral leg strength and balance
- Landmine Squat: Barbell-based alternative with minimal spinal load

sections.heading: Belt Squat Variations
sections.content:
Standard Belt Squat: Shoulder-width stance, full range of motion
Wide Stance Belt Squat: Greater adductor and glute emphasis
Close Stance Belt Squat: Greater quad emphasis
Tempo Belt Squat: Slow eccentric for hypertrophy
Pause Belt Squat: Pause at the bottom for strength and control
Single-Leg Belt Squat: Advanced unilateral variation

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Issues: Belt squat is already a good alternative; keep load moderate and control depth
Knee Pain: Reduce depth, use a narrower stance, focus on tempo
Hip Mobility Issues: Work on mobility drills; limit depth to pain-free range
No Belt Squat Machine: Use landmine squats, hack squat, or leg press as substitutes
Balance Issues: Hold the machine handles lightly for stability
Beginners: Start with light resistance and learn the movement pattern first
